title: 'Abasa: he frowned
hook: the Prophet ﷺ turned from a blind man to talk to the powerful, and was corrected (80:1–10)
carry: turn to the one who came

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, and the buried girl who is given the question. Your line was she will be asked.

A work event. You're finally talking to the one person in the room who could change everything: the investor, the boss's boss, the person with the answer. Then a tap on your shoulder. The intern, or an old neighbor, asking a question that could wait. You don't say anything rude. Your face just does a small thing. A flicker. A frown. It would be easy never to think about it again. The surah just before At-Takwir is named after that flicker. And the surprise is whose face it was. Today: 'Abasa, he frowned.
screen: `FINALLY TALKING TO THE RIGHT PERSON.` → `A TAP ON THE SHOULDER.` → `'ABASA, HE FROWNED.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty opens, in Pickthall's words: He frowned and turned away Because the blind man came unto him. Sunni commentators, following reports in Tirmidhi and the tafsir, explain the scene this way. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was in Mecca, speaking with leaders of the Quraysh, hoping they would listen. A blind man, 'Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came up asking to be taught. The Prophet frowned and turned back to the leaders, and revelation came correcting him. Shia commentators such as al-Tabataba'i, and some others, read it differently: the one who frowned was another man present, not the Prophet. Both readings are held with care. Now listen to how the correction is spoken. It begins in the third person, he frowned, which commentators read as courtesy, the text almost looking away. Then it speaks directly: what could tell you, perhaps he would grow in purity, or be reminded, and the reminder would help him. As for the one who thinks he needs nothing, you give him your attention. But the one who came to you eagerly, and in awe, him you neglect. And the correction stays in the text, recited ever since. What happened next? Ibn Umm Maktum became a caller to prayer in Medina, alongside Bilal, and reports say the Prophet left him in charge of the prayer in Medina when he traveled. The man turned away from became the voice calling the city to prayer.
screen: `HE FROWNED AND TURNED AWAY.` · `IBN UMM MAKTUM, WHO CAME TO LEARN.` · `A CORRECTION KEPT IN THE TEXT.` · `THE VOICE THAT CALLED MEDINA.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE ONE WHO CAME.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who come to you and are easy to overlook: the quiet coworker, the kid who wants to show you something, the older relative who repeats a story, the person at the counter. Pick one, and picture the next time they come to you, and you turn fully toward them: phone down, eyes up, full attention.
'Abasa. He frowned, the name of Surah eighty, which turns our attention to the one who came eagerly. Today's word.
Your line: turn to the one who came. The eager one was the one to turn to. That's day two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 'Abasa as a lesson that sincerity outweighs status; Ibn Umm Maktum is remembered as a companion and muezzin, and the surah sits in Juz' 'Amma, the thirtieth part of the Qur'an, often learned by heart early.

original.note: Arabic: "he frowned," the first word and the name of Surah 80.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah where someone was rude.
what it means: a frown at an eager blind man, corrected by revelation: attention belongs with the one who came.

what a scholar hears: the shift from third person ('abasa) to second person (wa ma yudrika) is read as courtesy in the rebuke; Tirmidhi 3331 on the occasion; Bukhari 617 on Ibn Umm Maktum's adhan; the Shia reading of the frowner differs.
